title: Z3 FOL API, OpenRouter Pricing, Few-Shot Prompts, and FOL Model Checker for Neuro-Symbolic World-Probing Experiment
summary: Four concrete implementation blocks for the heterogeneous-oracle world-probing experiment: (1) Verified Z3 Python entailment pattern using push/pop scoping and unsat checking; critical finding that LINC uses Prover9 not Z3. (2) OpenRouter pricing confirmed: Llama-3.1-8B at $0.02/$0.03 per 1M tokens, Qwen2.5-7B at $0.04/$0.10; free Qwen tier exists, total experiment cost ~$0.37 under $10 cap. (3) LINC few-shot prompt format with HTML-style tags and NLTK logic module FOL syntax extracted from paper appendix and FOLIO data. (4) Z3-based finite-domain FOL model checker algorithm with CWA enforcement and pure Python recursive alternative.
answer:
**Block 1: Z3 Python API for FOL Entailment**

The standard Z3 entailment check uses push/pop scoping [2][3]: add all premises with s.add(), then s.push(), add Not(conclusion), call s.check() — if unsat return 'Entailment'. Pop, push again, add conclusion, check — if unsat return 'Contradiction'. Otherwise 'Neutral'. Key Z3 primitives confirmed [2]: DeclareSort('Domain') for custom sorts, Function('Student', Domain, BoolSort()) for unary predicates, Function('Reads', Domain, Domain, BoolSort()) for binary relations, Const('alice', Domain) for named individuals, ForAll([x], Implies(P(x), Q(x))) for universal quantification, Exists([x], And(P(x), Q(x))) for existential quantification.

Critical discovery [1]: LINC (Olausson et al. EMNLP 2023) uses **Prover9** (not Z3) as its theorem prover backend, with NLTK logic module syntax ('all x. (P(x) -> Q(x))'). Z3 is the preferred choice for our experiment due to Python-native integration. The standard entailment-by-negation proof pattern is documented in Z3 guides [3][9]: 'F is valid precisely when Not(F) is not satisfiable.'

Complete entailment function:
```python
from z3 import *
def check_entailment(premise_formulas, conclusion_formula):
    s = Solver()
    for p in premise_formulas:
        s.add(p)
    s.push()
    s.add(Not(conclusion_formula))
    if s.check() == unsat:
        s.pop(); return 'Entailment'
    s.pop()
    s.push()
    s.add(conclusion_formula)
    if s.check() == unsat:
        s.pop(); return 'Contradiction'
    s.pop()
    return 'Neutral'
```

**Block 2: OpenRouter Model IDs and Pricing**

Verified 2026-06-09 [4][5][6]: meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct costs $0.02/1M input and $0.03/1M output with 131K context window [4]. qwen/qwen-2.5-7b-instruct costs $0.04/1M input and $0.10/1M output with 131K context [5]. A free tier qwen/qwen-2.5-7b-instruct:free exists with 2 providers at $0.00/$0.00, 131K context [6]. Both paid models confirmed available with multiple provider fallbacks.

Budget at paid rates: Step 0 (50ex Llama) ~$0.004, Step 1 (30ex Qwen pilot) ~$0.016, Step 2 Llama generation ~$0.016, Step 2 Qwen world generation ~$0.18, Step 2 Qwen oracle ~$0.13, Step 3 baselines ~$0.022, total ~$0.37 — leaving $9.63 headroom under the $10 cap. Using the free Qwen tier for oracle calls reduces total to ~$0.02–$0.05 [6].

**Block 3: Few-Shot NL-to-FOL Prompt Template**

LINC Appendix D.4 [1] specifies the neurosymbolic prompt format with an instruction prefix ('Expressions should adhere to the format of the Python NLTK package logic module') and HTML-style tags: <PREMISES>...</PREMISES>, <CONCLUSION>...</CONCLUSION>, <EVALUATE>TEXT: {nl}\nFOL: {fol}...</EVALUATE>. The <EVALUATE> block is the generation target; the LLM generates autoregressively until the closing tag.

FOL syntax is NLTK logic module [1]: universal 'all x. (P(x) -> Q(x))', existential 'exists x. (P(x) & Q(x))', negation '-P(x)', conjunction '&', implication '->'. Constants are CamelCase (e.g., Harry, Worksheet); predicates are CamelCase (e.g., Dispensable, EnvironmentFriendly).

Verified NL-to-FOL pairs from LINC paper [1]: 'All dispensable things are env-friendly.' -> 'all x. (Dispensable(x) -> EnvironmentFriendly(x))'; 'No good things are bad.' -> 'all x. (Good(x) -> -Bad(x))'; 'When a person reads a book, they gain knowledge.' -> 'all x. all y. (Person(x) & Reads(x,y) & Book(y) -> Gains(x,Knowledge))'. Additional pairs from FOLIO validation data [7]: 'If people perform in talent shows, they are engaged.' -> 'all x. (TalentShows(x) -> Engaged(x))'; 'Monkeypox occurs in some animals.' -> 'exists x. (Animal(x) & OccurMonkeypoxVirus(x))'.

LINC uses 8 hand-picked diverse FOLIO training samples as ICL examples, selected from indices 126, 24, 61, 276, 149, 262, 264, 684 of the FOLIO training set [1]. The most common LLM error is using the same predicate symbol with multiple arities: 38% StarCoder+, 24% GPT-3.5, 13% GPT-4 [1].

**Block 4: Python FOL Model Checker Design**

Recommended approach is Z3-based [2][8] since Z3 is already required for entailment checking. World model format: {'entities': ['alice', 'bob'], 'atoms': {'Student': [['alice']], 'Reads': [['alice', 'logic_book']]}}. Algorithm: (1) DeclareSort('Domain'), (2) add finite-domain axiom ForAll([x], Or(*[x==c for c in named_constants])), (3) assert all ground atoms and CWA negations for unlisted atoms, (4) evaluate formula by checking if Not(formula) is unsat [2][3].

Pure Python tuple-AST recursive evaluator also works without Z3 dependencies. Formula types: ('atom', pred, args), ('not', f), ('and', f1, f2), ('or', f1, f2), ('implies', ant, cons), ('forall', var, body), ('exists', var, body). ForAll evaluates as all(eval(body, {var: e}) for e in entities); Exists as any(...) [8].

Known edge cases [1][2]: arity mismatch (most common LLM error), equality requires special handling, CWA must be explicitly enforced, domain finiteness constraint is critical for Z3 termination, XOR vs OR ambiguity for 'either...or' statements in FOLIO, lowercase vs uppercase convention (lowercase=variable, uppercase=constant in NLTK syntax).
